title: When the lesion is everywhere: coma and diffuse disease
description: How to localize a child who cannot cooperate. The module covers the two structures that sustain consciousness, the coma examination as a way of finding the level, metabolic versus structural coma, herniation, and diffuse disease.
why: Some findings refuse to point to a single level, and recognizing that pattern is itself a localization.
objectives: Explain why depressed consciousness localizes to the brainstem tegmentum or to both hemispheres, and what a one-sided lesion must do to cause coma.
Use breathing, pupils, eye movements and motor responses to place a coma at one level, or to recognize that the signs do not agree.
Separate metabolic and toxic coma from structural coma at the bedside, and act on the difference.
Recognize uncal herniation from the pupil, and explain why the hemiparesis may sit on the wrong side.
Treat diffuse and multifocal disease in a child as an address in its own right, and carry it into a differential.

sections.title: The two structures that sustain consciousness
sections.content:
Every other module in this curriculum asks the patient to do something, such as squeezing your fingers, following a target, walking across the room or reporting a pinprick. A child in coma can do none of these things, so you have to localize from the reflexes and from the level of consciousness itself.

**The brainstem and both hemispheres**

Wakefulness depends on the **ascending reticular activating system** in the brainstem working together with the **cerebral hemispheres**. In people the activating system lies in the paramedian tegmentum of the pons and midbrain (Brazis 2011, p. 604). Coma therefore has only two true addresses in the brain. One is a lesion in that small tegmental core, and the other is dysfunction of **both** hemispheres at once.

A lesion confined to **one hemisphere** does not abolish consciousness on its own. A child with a large one-sided stroke or tumor may be aphasic, hemiplegic and miserable, and still be awake. If that child becomes unresponsive, something has changed. The lesion may have grown or swollen enough to press on the brainstem, a second process may have appeared on the other side, or the child may be having seizures without convulsions. Unresponsiveness in a child with a one-sided lesion is a **new localizing sign**, and usually an emergency.

**Describing responsiveness**

Words such as lethargic, obtunded and stuporous sound precise, but they carry little of the information needed for localization. Describe responsiveness in plain words instead, recording the stimulus you used and exactly how the child responded (Brazis 2011, p. 603). The next examiner can compare their own findings with a note that reads "Opened her eyes to her name, looked at her mother, then drifted off without speaking." A note that reads "lethargic" gives them nothing to compare. In a child the useful stimuli include a parent's voice, a favorite toy or a feed.

The rest of this module applies the same habit to the brainstem reflexes, which keep working when the child cannot cooperate. It then turns to the diffuse diseases, where "everywhere" is a genuine answer.
keyPoints: Consciousness needs the brainstem reticular activating system (paramedian tegmentum of the pons and midbrain) and both hemispheres (Brazis 2011, p. 604).
A lesion confined to one hemisphere does not cause coma on its own, so coma in that setting suggests brainstem compression, a second lesion or non-convulsive seizures.
Describe responsiveness in plain words, naming the stimulus and the response, rather than with labels such as lethargic or stuporous (Brazis 2011, p. 603).
When the child cannot cooperate, the brainstem reflexes become the examination.

question.question: A 9-year-old with a known left frontal tumor has been awake and talking with a right hemiparesis. Overnight she becomes hard to rouse, opening her eyes only to a firm sternal rub and not speaking. What does the change in consciousness tell you?
options: Nothing new about localization, since the tumor is in the left hemisphere and hemispheric lesions cause sleepiness
A new process is involving the brainstem or the other hemisphere, such as swelling with herniation or non-convulsive seizures, and it needs urgent assessment
The tumor has spread along the corticospinal tract, which explains both the weakness and the drowsiness
She is post-ictal after an unwitnessed seizure, so observation without imaging is appropriate
question.explanation: Consciousness needs the brainstem activating system and both hemispheres, so a lesion confined to one hemisphere does not abolish it. Unresponsiveness in a child with a one-sided tumor means something new, such as swelling that compresses the brainstem or seizures without convulsions. Spread along the corticospinal tract could not explain coma. A post-ictal state is a conclusion reached only after excluding herniation and ongoing seizures.

sections.title: Finding the level in coma
sections.content:
The four signs that need no effort from the child are the **pattern of breathing**, the **pupils**, the **eye movements** and the **motor response to pain**. Each changes in a characteristic way from one level to the next (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-97). Set each sign in the figure above to see whether they agree.

**Breathing.** Breathing that waxes and wanes with pauses in between (Cheyne-Stokes) points to both hemispheres or the diencephalon. Sustained, fast, deep breathing, once acidosis and lung disease are excluded, points to the brainstem from the low midbrain to the middle of the pons. Long pauses at full inspiration (apneustic breathing) point to the pons. Chaotic, irregular breathing points to the medulla, where the respiratory rhythm is generated (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-95).

**Pupils.** Small pupils that still react fit diencephalic or metabolic depression (Brazis 2011, p. 608). A midbrain lesion interrupts the light reflex, so the pupils lose their reactivity. A pontine lesion cuts the descending sympathetic fibers and leaves the pupils pinpoint (Pearl 2014, p. 95), although they still react to light if you look closely (Brazis 2011, p. 608).

**Eye movements.** When you turn the head of a comatose child whose brainstem is intact, the eyes move the opposite way and keep pointing in the same direction in space, the doll's-eye movement (Pearl 2014, p. 96). Do not turn the head if the neck may be injured. Cold water in the ear is a stronger stimulus, and if both eyes turn toward the cold ear the brainstem from the upper medulla to the midbrain is working. In coma there is no corrective fast phase, so the eyes deviate slowly without nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

**Motor response.** Flexion of the arms with extended legs places the lesion between the cortex and the upper midbrain. Extension of all four limbs places it between the midbrain and the pontomedullary junction, and flaccidity places it below that (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

**Putting it together.** If all four signs point to the same level, a single structural lesion there fits. If they **disagree**, the process is probably multifocal, and multifocal coma is most often metabolic. If they **move downward** over hours, think of herniation (Pearl 2014, p. 97). Children are scored with modified versions of the adult coma scales (Pearl 2014, p. 147), and the logic of finding the level is the same at every age.
keyPoints: Breathing, pupils, eye movements and motor responses each point to a level, and all four keep working when the child cannot cooperate (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-97).
Pinpoint pupils with apneustic breathing and absent horizontal eye movements point to the pons, while small reactive pupils fit diencephalic or metabolic depression (Brazis 2011, p. 608).
Eyes that turn toward cold water in the ear show that the brainstem from medulla to midbrain is working.
Signs that agree suggest one structural lesion, signs that disagree suggest multifocal and usually metabolic disease, and signs that move downward suggest herniation (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

question.question: A 12-year-old is found unresponsive. She has long pauses at the top of each breath, pinpoint pupils, no horizontal eye movement when the head is turned, and extends all four limbs to pain. Where is the lesion, and what kind of process does the pattern suggest?
options: Both hemispheres, from a metabolic cause, because she is in coma
The medulla, because breathing is abnormal
The pons, from a single structural lesion, because every sign points to the same level
The midbrain, because extensor posturing always means a midbrain lesion
question.explanation: Apneustic breathing, pinpoint pupils, absent horizontal doll's-eye movements and extensor posturing all point to the pons, and when every sign agrees on one level a single structural lesion there fits best. Metabolic coma gives small reactive pupils and intact doll's eyes. Medullary breathing is chaotic. Extensor posturing spans the midbrain to the pontomedullary junction, so it cannot pin the lesion to the midbrain.

sections.title: Metabolic or structural?
sections.content:
At the bedside of a comatose child, the most useful early decision concerns the **kind** of problem more than its level. Either a structural lesion is damaging or compressing the brain, or the brain is being poisoned or starved. The two are managed differently, and a poisoned or starved brain can sometimes be helped within minutes.

**Pupils and eye movements**

In metabolic coma the **pupils may still react when the eye movements are gone** (Brazis 2011, p. 610). The pupillary light reflex is one of the most resistant reflexes in the brainstem, so a drug or a metabolic derangement can silence the eye movements while the small pupils still constrict to light. A structural brainstem lesion severe enough to abolish the eye movements usually changes the pupils as well, leaving them fixed in mid-position or dilated after midbrain damage, or pinpoint after pontine damage (Pearl 2014, p. 95). Small, briskly reactive pupils with absent eye movements point toward a toxic or metabolic cause.

**Drugs and the pupils**

Drugs can do almost anything to the pupils (Pearl 2014, p. 96). Anticholinergics and stimulants dilate them, and barbiturates, benzodiazepines and other sedatives constrict them. Opioids and clonidine can make them pinpoint, much like a pontine lesion. Most sedative overdoses do not abolish the light reflex (Brazis 2011, p. 608). A toddler who has found a grandparent's tablets can produce a coma examination that mimics almost any level.

**Signs of a structural cause**

Asymmetry favors a structural cause, whether it shows as unequal pupils, a gaze deviation, a hemiparesis or posturing on one side. So does a pattern that **descends** over hours. Symmetry, fluctuation and signs that disagree about the level point toward a toxic or metabolic cause (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

**In a child**

The metabolic list in children is long and urgent. It includes low glucose, ingestion, high ammonia, diabetic ketoacidosis, infection and non-convulsive seizures. Only an EEG can confirm non-convulsive seizures, so request one early (the [EEG curriculum](/eeg) covers how to read it). Check the glucose at once, because low glucose can itself cause focal signs. Look for a chemical cause while you examine, and image urgently whenever the examination is asymmetric or worsening.
keyPoints: Reactive pupils with absent eye movements are the classic sign of metabolic or toxic coma (Brazis 2011, p. 610).
Drugs can do anything to the pupils, with anticholinergics and stimulants dilating them and sedatives constricting them (Pearl 2014, p. 96).
Asymmetry and a descending pattern point to a structural lesion, while symmetry and signs that disagree point to metabolic disease.
In every comatose child, check the glucose immediately and look for a chemical cause while the examination proceeds.

question.question: A 2-year-old is brought in very drowsy after playing unsupervised at a relative's house. Her pupils are small and react briskly to light, she has no horizontal eye movement on head turning, and her limbs are symmetrically floppy. What is the most appropriate interpretation and first step?
options: A pontine hemorrhage, because horizontal eye movements are absent; arrange neurosurgical review before anything else
Probably toxic or metabolic, because the pupils react despite absent eye movements; check the glucose at once and start a toxic and metabolic search, imaging if anything becomes asymmetric
Brain death must be considered, because the doll's-eye response is absent
A functional unresponsiveness, because the examination is symmetric
question.explanation: Reactive pupils despite absent eye movements point to toxic or metabolic coma, and after unsupervised play an ingestion heads the list. Check the glucose first, then screen for toxic and metabolic causes, and image if the signs become asymmetric. A pontine hemorrhage gives pinpoint pupils and usually abnormal breathing or posturing. Brain death requires absent pupillary reflexes. A symmetric exam is typical of metabolic coma.

sections.title: Herniation: when the lesion moves
sections.content:
A growing mass in a closed skull pushes brain from one compartment into another. The signs then come from the place being squeezed, so the localization itself moves while you watch.

**Uncal herniation and the pupil**

An expanding mass in or beside one temporal lobe, such as a hematoma, can push the uncus over the edge of the tentorium and onto the third nerve and the midbrain (Pearl 2014, pp. 37, 93). The pupil-constricting fibers run on the outside of the third nerve, so external pressure dilates the pupil early, on the **same side** as the mass, before a progressive third-nerve palsy and falling consciousness.

The side of the hemiparesis is a less reliable guide. You would expect the mass to weaken the opposite side, because it presses on the corticospinal fibers on its own side. But the shifted midbrain can be pushed against the far edge of the tentorium, which notches the other cerebral peduncle (Kernohan's notch) and weakens the limbs on the **same side** as the mass. In uncal herniation the dilated pupil reliably shows the side of the lesion, and the hemiparesis may not (Pearl 2014, p. 37).

**Other forms of herniation**

The cingulate gyrus can slide under the falx and compress the anterior cerebral artery, which weakens the opposite leg. Swelling of both hemispheres pushes the diencephalon straight down and causes progressive dysfunction of both sides of the brainstem from the top. Cerebellar tonsils pushed through the foramen magnum compress the medulla, and breathing and circulation can then fail abruptly (Pearl 2014, pp. 92-93). A slowing pulse with a widening pulse pressure and a change in breathing is a late sign of raised pressure (Pearl 2014, p. 94), so do not wait for it.

**Following the coma signs**

The coma signs from section 2 are the best way to watch for herniation. Breathing may change from Cheyne-Stokes to sustained hyperventilation, the pupils from small and reactive to fixed, and posturing from flexion to extension. Treat a level that descends over hours as herniation unless something else clearly explains it (Pearl 2014, p. 97). To see the sequence, press **Watch a herniation descend** in the coma figure in section 2. Posterior fossa tumors are common in children, so downward herniation of the cerebellar tonsils is a particular concern, and a lumbar puncture in a child with a mass and signs of raised pressure can set it off.
keyPoints: In uncal herniation the pupil on the side of the mass dilates first, because the pupillary fibers run on the outside of the third nerve (Pearl 2014, pp. 36-37).
The hemiparesis can be on the same side as the mass (Kernohan's notch), so the pupil is the more reliable guide to the side (Pearl 2014, p. 37).
Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla and can stop breathing and circulation abruptly (Pearl 2014, p. 93).
A level that descends over hours on serial coma examinations should be treated as herniation unless something else clearly explains it (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

question.question: A 14-year-old is brought in after a fall from a bicycle. He was talking, then became drowsy. His right pupil is dilated and sluggish, and his RIGHT arm and leg are weaker than the left. On which side is the expanding lesion most likely to be?
options: Left, because the hemiparesis is on the right and the corticospinal tract crosses
It cannot be told, because the signs conflict
Both sides equally, so bilateral surgery should be planned
Right, because the dilated pupil reliably marks the side of uncal herniation, and the same-side weakness can come from the opposite peduncle being notched on the tentorium
question.explanation: In uncal herniation the pupil-constricting fibers on the outside of the third nerve are compressed first, so the dilated pupil is on the side of the mass. Same-side weakness comes from the opposite peduncle being pressed against the tentorium (Kernohan's notch), which is why the pupil is the more reliable sign. Reading the weakness in the usual crossed way sends you to the wrong side.

sections.title: False localizing signs
sections.content:
Some signs mislead you about where the lesion is. A **false localizing sign** is caused by a process at a distance, through pressure, shift or a drug, rather than by damage at the place the sign usually points to.

**The sixth nerve**

[[m07-brainstem|Module 7]] introduced a child with morning headaches, vomiting and double vision on looking to one side. The sixth nerve has a long course and is an early casualty of raised intracranial pressure, whether from a tumor above or below the tentorium, hydrocephalus or pseudotumor cerebri (Pearl 2014, pp. 43, 48; Brazis 2011, p. 202). Sixth-nerve palsy and papilledema are the commonest false localizing signs (Brazis 2011, p. 622). A supratentorial process, especially a midline one causing hydrocephalus, can raise the pressure without focal signs and leave cranial nerve palsies that look like a posterior fossa lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 622). Posterior fossa tumors are common in children (Pearl 2014, p. 63), so the posterior fossa is a fair suspect, but a sixth-nerve palsy here tells you only that the pressure is raised.

**Other false localizing signs**

- **The wrong-sided hemiparesis** of Kernohan's notch, already met in the herniation section (Brazis 2011, p. 616).
- **A sensory level that is too low**, when compression high in the cervical cord gives a sensory level on the trunk together with clumsy, wasted hands (Brazis 2011, p. 115).
- **Nystagmus from drugs**, since anticonvulsants can produce a central-looking nystagmus with no lesion in the brainstem (Pearl 2014, p. 121).
- **Anomia**, because word-finding failure is relatively nonlocalizing (Pearl 2014, p. 20; [[m09-hemispheres|Module 9]]).

**Vertical gaze**

Vertical gaze is different, because a tumor pressing on the posterior commissure, such as a pineal tumor, disturbs it directly. It can hold the eyes tonically downward, as part of Parinaud syndrome (Pearl 2014, p. 40). In a child with raised pressure, failure of upgaze points to the dorsal midbrain. Hydrocephalus can also press on the dorsal midbrain, which is why an infant with rising pressure may show downward-deviated "setting sun" eyes.

:::deeper Telling a cortical gaze palsy from a pontine one
When the eyes rest deviated to one side, turn the head passively. The doll's-eye movement overcomes the gaze preference of a cortical lesion, because the brainstem gaze center still works. It cannot overcome the gaze palsy of a pontine lesion, because that center is gone (Pearl 2014, p. 45). The eyes look toward a destructive cortical lesion and away from a pontine one (Pearl 2014, p. 43), so this one maneuver tells you both the level and the side.
:::

**Checking a sign against its companions**

Be suspicious of a sign that turns up without its usual companions. Ask which other signs it would bring if the lesion were really at that site. If those signs are missing, consider pressure, shift or a drug as the cause, and image the whole head rather than only the spot the sign seems to point to.
keyPoints: A false localizing sign is caused at a distance, by pressure, shift or a drug, rather than by damage at the place it usually points to.
Sixth-nerve palsy and papilledema are the commonest false localizing signs, and a supratentorial or midline process can imitate a posterior fossa lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 622).

Kernohan's notch, a sensory level from high cervical compression, drug-induced nystagmus and anomia all point to the wrong place or to nowhere in particular (Brazis 2011, pp. 115, 616; Pearl 2014, pp. 20, 121).
Failure of vertical gaze from pressure on the posterior commissure does localize, to the pineal region (Pearl 2014, p. 40).
Passive head turning overcomes a cortical gaze preference but not a pontine gaze palsy (Pearl 2014, p. 45).

question.question: An 8-year-old has had three weeks of morning headaches and vomiting. Both optic discs are swollen and neither eye abducts fully. There is no facial weakness, no gaze palsy, no ataxia and no long-tract sign. A colleague requests an MRI limited to the pons and posterior fossa. What do you advise?
options: Agree, because posterior fossa tumors are common in children and the sixth nerves arise from the pons
Do a lumbar puncture first to measure the opening pressure, then decide on imaging
Image the orbits to look for disease of the lateral rectus muscles
Image the whole brain urgently, because bilateral sixth-nerve palsies with papilledema report raised pressure, which a supratentorial or midline process can cause as readily as a posterior fossa one
question.explanation: Sixth-nerve palsy and papilledema are the commonest false localizing signs, because the long sixth nerve suffers from raised pressure from any source, and a supratentorial or midline lesion can imitate a posterior fossa one (Brazis 2011, p. 622; Pearl 2014, p. 43). A limited scan could miss the cause. A lumbar puncture first risks herniation, and swollen discs mean the problem is inside the skull.

sections.title: Diffuse and multifocal disease in children
sections.content:
Localization trains you to look for the single point where the findings meet, and sometimes there is no such point. The answer is then "everywhere", which narrows the differential as sharply as any single level on the [[m01-where-before-what|map of levels]].

**Discrete lesions and system disease**

Much of localization was learned from discrete lesions such as infarcts, tumors, abscesses and demyelinating plaques. Other diseases attack whole arrays of neurons that share a function (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Discrete lesions give signs that meet at one point. System diseases give signs that follow a system, a tract or a cell type instead of a place.

**Diffuse, multifocal and system disease**

- **Diffuse:** an encephalopathy from a toxin, an infection, a metabolic derangement or prolonged seizures, in which consciousness falls, the signs are symmetric, and the coma examination does not settle on a level.
- **Multifocal:** several discrete lesions at once, as in acute disseminated encephalomyelitis after an infection, the classic pediatric example, where a sleepy child has signs from the hemispheres, the brainstem and the cord that no single lesion can explain.
- **System:** a genetic or metabolic disease that takes one kind of tissue throughout the nervous system, such as the white matter in a leukodystrophy or the gray matter in a neuronal storage disease.

**Regression: localization in time**

In a child, "everywhere" often shows itself as a loss of skills rather than a coma. Regression places the process in time as clearly as a sensory level places it in space, because it shows that the disease is active now. It also moves the differential toward neurodegenerative, genetic and metabolic causes, the epileptic encephalopathies and acquired encephalitis.

Once you have named the pattern as diffuse, multifocal or system, use the tempo of the illness to choose among the causes, with the grid that [[m11-where-to-what|Module 11]] builds.
keyPoints: "Everywhere" is itself a localization, because diffuse, multifocal and system patterns each narrow the differential.
Discrete lesions give signs that meet at a point, whereas system diseases give signs that respect a tract or cell type throughout the nervous system (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
Signs from several levels at once in a sleepy child after an infection suggest a multifocal process such as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
Regression, the loss of skills already acquired, localizes a process in time and points toward neurodegenerative, genetic and metabolic causes and epileptic encephalopathy.

question.question: A 6-year-old became sleepy and irritable ten days after a viral illness. She now has a mild left hemiparesis, unsteady arms, double vision and difficulty passing urine. No single lesion explains all of this. What is the most useful way to frame her localization?
options: Multifocal central nervous system disease, which points toward an acute inflammatory demyelinating process and calls for imaging of the brain and the whole spine
Brainstem, because double vision is present, so imaging of the posterior fossa alone is enough
Non-localizing, so localization adds nothing and broad testing should replace it
Peripheral nerve, because the bladder is involved
question.explanation: Signs from a hemisphere (the hemiparesis), the brainstem or cerebellar connections (double vision, unsteadiness) and the cord (the bladder) cannot come from one lesion. Multifocal disease after an infection points to acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, so image the brain and whole spine. A posterior fossa scan could miss the cord, and a nerve problem cannot explain drowsiness.

quiz.question: A 4-year-old is comatose after a cardiac arrest. Breathing is Cheyne-Stokes, the pupils are small and reactive, the eyes move fully with head turning, and the arms flex to pain. A colleague asks where the lesion is. What is the best answer?
options: The medulla, because breathing is irregular
Both hemispheres or the diencephalon, with the brainstem working, because every sign points to that level
The pons, because the pupils are small
The midbrain, because there is posturing
quiz.explanation: Cheyne-Stokes breathing, small reactive pupils, intact doll's-eye movements and flexor posturing all point above the midbrain, to both hemispheres or the diencephalon with a working brainstem, which fits a diffuse hypoxic insult. Medullary breathing is chaotic. Pontine pupils are pinpoint, and pontine lesions abolish horizontal doll's-eye movements. Flexor posturing agrees with the hemispheric level.

quiz.question: An adolescent is comatose. His pupils react to light, but cold water in either ear produces no eye movement at all, and his limbs are symmetrically flaccid. Breathing is shallow but regular. What does this combination suggest?
options: A structural lesion of the whole brainstem, so the outlook is hopeless
Brain death, because there is no caloric response
A toxic or metabolic cause such as a sedative overdose, because the pupils still react when the eye movements are gone
Locked-in syndrome, because he is not moving
quiz.explanation: The pupillary light reflex is among the most resistant brainstem reflexes, so reactive pupils with absent calorics point toward a drug or metabolic cause, which may be fully reversible. A structural lesion destroying the brainstem would usually take the pupils too, so calling the outlook hopeless is dangerous. Brain death requires absent pupillary reflexes. A locked-in patient is awake.

quiz.question: A child with a left temporal abscess becomes drowsy. Over two hours his breathing changes from waxing and waning to fast and deep, the left pupil enlarges and stops reacting, and his flexor posturing becomes extensor. What is happening?
options: Transtentorial herniation, because the level of dysfunction is descending through the brainstem
Recovery, because his breathing is now regular
A new seizure focus in the right hemisphere
A medullary stroke, because breathing has changed
quiz.explanation: Each sign has moved down a level, with breathing shifting from the hemispheric to the midbrain pattern, the pupil from reactive to fixed and posture from flexion to extension. A level that descends over hours is herniation, and a dilating pupil on the side of the abscess fits uncal herniation. Deep regular breathing here reflects midbrain involvement and is no sign of recovery.

quiz.question: A resident writes "patient obtunded" in a sedated child's notes. Why does the attending ask for a rewrite?
options: Because obtunded is the wrong grade; the child is stuporous
Because sedated children cannot be assessed
Because labels such as obtunded mean different things to different readers; describing the stimulus and the response lets the next examiner tell whether the child has changed
Because only the coma scale score should be written
quiz.explanation: Describe responsiveness in plain words, recording the stimulus and exactly what the child did (Brazis 2011, p. 603). Labels such as obtunded are applied inconsistently, so they cannot show change between examinations, which is the point of serial assessment. Sedated children can still be assessed, with the sedation recorded, and a coma score loses details such as which side moves.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old has two weeks of morning headaches and vomiting. She cannot look up, her eyes rest slightly downward, and she has a mild left sixth-nerve palsy. Which finding best tells you where the lesion is?
options: The failure of upgaze, which points to pressure on the posterior commissure in the pineal region
The left sixth-nerve palsy, which places the lesion in the left pons
Neither, because once the pressure is raised every eye sign is a false localizing sign
The vomiting, which places the lesion in the medulla
quiz.explanation: A tumor pressing on the posterior commissure, such as a pineal tumor, disturbs vertical gaze and can hold the eyes down (Pearl 2014, p. 40), so failure of upgaze is a true address. The sixth nerve suffers from raised pressure of any cause and is the commonest false localizing sign (Pearl 2014, p. 43; Brazis 2011, p. 622).

signOff: The resident examines a child with depressed consciousness, describes responsiveness in plain words, and states the level of the lesion or that the process is diffuse, with a faculty reader.

opener.parable: Sometimes the examination refuses to settle on a single level. The pupils point one way, the breathing another and the eye movements somewhere else again. That disagreement is useful in its own right, because it usually means something is affecting the whole brain at once.
opener.history: The warning triad of rising intracranial pressure (a slowing pulse, a widening pulse pressure and a change in breathing) carries the name of Harvey Cushing.
